sections.title: Diabetes mellitus
summary: ACS patients with diabetes mellitus (DM) may present with non-specific symptoms leading to delays in diagnosis and treatment; they tend to have more advanced CAD at diagnosis and worse long-term prognosis, particularly if requiring insulin.
All ACS patients should have glycaemic status evaluated during hospitalization; diagnoses of DM made during hospitalisation should be confirmed later because ACS can cause stress hyperglycaemia.

Management of hyperglycaemia (>11.0 mmol/L or 200 mg/dL) in hospitalized ACS patients has shown benefits, but intensive insulin therapy increases risk of hypoglycaemia and this risk should not be neglected.

Glucose-lowering reduces microvascular complications. Recent trial evidence shows that SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 receptor agonists reduce risk of new ACS events, heart failure (HF), and renal impairment independent of baseline HbA1c.

These benefits should be considered when choosing glucose-lowering therapy for patients with DM and concomitant CAD; refer to 2023 ESC Guidelines on diabetes and cardiovascular disease and 2021 ESC Guidelines on cardiovascular disease prevention for details.

sections.title: Older adults with frailty and multimorbidity
summary: Older adults are an increasing proportion of ACS patients; age is a major predictor of adverse outcomes and patients aged ≥75 years are often under-represented in trials.
Older age is associated with frailty, multimorbidity, and greater risk of both ischaemic and bleeding events in ACS.

High-sensitivity cardiac troponin (hs-cTn) assays have excellent diagnostic performance in older persons but lower specificity than in younger patients; elevated cTn levels in older patients are often associated with conditions other than ACS.

sections.title: Renal considerations and hydration
summary: For ACS patients with low eGFR undergoing invasive management, intravenous hydration should be considered to minimize risk of contrast-induced nephropathy.
For long-term treatment in patients with ACS and concomitant chronic kidney disease (CKD) refer to the 2021 ESC Guidelines on cardiovascular disease prevention.

recommendations: Evaluate glycaemic status in all ACS patients during hospitalization and confirm in-hospital diagnoses of DM later.
Avoid neglecting the risk of hypoglycaemia when using intensive insulin therapy in hospitalized ACS patients.
Consider SGLT2 inhibitors or GLP-1 receptor agonists for reducing risk of new ACS events, HF, and renal impairment in patients with DM, independent of baseline HbA1c.
Consider IV hydration for patients with low eGFR undergoing invasive ACS management to reduce contrast-induced nephropathy risk.
Refer to the 2023 ESC Guidelines on diabetes and cardiovascular disease and the 2021 ESC Guidelines on cardiovascular disease prevention for further details.
